input:
The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in the study of convective heat transfer, and it can be understood, in essence, as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. In order to appreciate what this ratio really tells us, it is helpful to imagine the comparison being made for one and the same surface, subject to one and the same temperature difference, across one and the same layer of fluid: on the one hand there is the heat that is actually carried away from the surface when the fluid is moving, and on the other hand there is the heat that conduction alone would be able to carry across the layer if the fluid were perfectly still.

This ratio is typically built up from three ingredients, namely the surface heat transfer coefficient, which captures the strength of the convection, the thermal conductivity of the fluid, and a characteristic length associated with the surface, which together capture the strength of the conduction against which the convection is being compared. Because it is a ratio of two heat transfer rates, the Nusselt number carries no units, and its numerical value expresses the outcome of the comparison in a direct and intuitive way.

When the Nusselt number is near 1, this tells us that convection is adding almost nothing over and above conduction. At a value of 1, in other words, the moving fluid is transferring heat at essentially the same rate that pure conduction across the layer would deliver, almost as though the fluid were stagnant, and the dominant resistance to heat transfer resides within the fluid layer itself. When the Nusselt number is large, by contrast, the picture is completely reversed: convection is carrying heat away from the surface far more rapidly than conduction across the layer ever could, the temperature change is squeezed into a thin region of fluid immediately adjacent to the surface, and the resistance of the layer becomes comparatively small. It is worth noting that there is no single fixed threshold that separates these two regimes; rather, the number measures the enhancement over conduction, and its significance is judged by how far it rises above the conduction limit, underscoring the fundamental role that fluid motion plays in surface heat transfer.
target:
The Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The comparison is made for the same surface, the same temperature difference, and the same fluid layer. The numerator is the heat carried away from the surface with the fluid in motion. The denominator is the heat that conduction alone would carry across the layer if the fluid were still.

The number is formed from the surface heat transfer coefficient, the thermal conductivity of the fluid, and a characteristic length of the surface. The coefficient states the strength of the convection; the conductivity and the length state the strength of the conduction against which the convection is compared. The ratio is dimensionless, and its value states the outcome of the comparison directly.

A Nusselt number near 1 states that convection adds almost nothing to conduction. At a value of 1, the moving fluid transfers heat at the rate that pure conduction across the layer would give, as if the fluid were stagnant, and the resistance to heat transfer sits in the fluid layer itself. The surface is then, in thermal terms, insulated by its own fluid.

A large Nusselt number states the opposite condition. Convection carries heat away from the surface far faster than conduction across the layer could carry it. The temperature change is compressed into a thin region of fluid at the surface, and the resistance of the layer is small beside the transfer the motion sustains. No fixed value separates the two conditions; the number measures an enhancement over conduction, and its meaning is read from its distance above the conduction limit.

The Nusselt number therefore reports how much the motion of the fluid improves heat transfer at a surface over conduction alone. A value at the conduction limit and a large value are the two ends of one scale, and every reported value stands between them.
